newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Trouble warning as Madagascar awaits poll result.
newsitem.headline: Trouble warning as Madagascar awaits poll result.

text.p: Security forces on the island of Madagascar warned on Thursday against trouble when the long-awaited presidential election result is announced on Friday.
The armed forces, gendarmerie and police warning followed persistent rumours that supporters of the losing candidate would provoke unrest because the vote was so close.
In a statement, the security forces reminded the public the election was an expression of popular will and therefore it was only up to the law to decide on the regularity of the results.

The announcement of results was suspended early this month after most of them had been broadcast when former president Albert Zafy complained the figures were being manipulated in favour of his opponent, former military ruler Didier Ratsiraka.
When the announcements were halted, Ratsiraka led with 50.l per cent of the votes recorded, leaving him 32,000 votes ahead with only about 30,000 left to be counted.
The security forces said the High Constitutional Court alone could decide on the fairness of the election and vote count.
"The forces of order will not hesitate to apply with firmness all necessary measures to block all subversive activities...to maintain and if necessary re-establish public order", they said.
Following the proclamation of results by the High Constitutional Court, interim President Norbert Ratsirahonana is expected to present the resignation of his government.
The rival parties have both said they will accept the verdict of the voters.
Election observers from the Organisation of African Unity, the International Committee of Jurists and the Francophone Agency for Technical and Cultural Cooperation have said the election was normal.
The December 29 run-off was necessary because none of 15 candidates in a first poll received 50 percent of the vote.
The early presidential poll was ordered after the national assembly impeached Zafy, 69, in July last year for contravening the constitution and exceeding his constitutional powers.
Ratsiraka, 60, campaigned on promises of establishing a "humanistic and ecological republic" in Madagascar, the world's fourth largest island where 14 million people live in chronic poverty.
Ratsiraka was reviled by many of his people in the early 1990s for using the army to resist the pro-democracy movement. He was beaten by Zafy in presidential elections in 1993 after a wave of unrest.
